_note: Starting points for the Add connector form. 'tested' means it was connected and exercised on this system; 'template' means it has NOT been run here and needs the owner's account or credential. Facts were read from each project's repository and README on 2026-10-11; check the README for the current flags.

templates.title: Time and time zones (official reference server)
templates.summary: Current time in any time zone and conversion between zones. Needs no account, no credential and no network: the safest first connector.

definition.name: time
definition.label: Time and time zones
definition.purpose: Current time and time-zone conversion (read only).

setup: Install it into its own folder (not the kernel's Python): python -m venv D:\jarvis\tools\mcp-venv, then D:\jarvis\tools\mcp-venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install mcp-server-time.
Press Add connector, then Test connection: its two tools appear switched off.
Classify get_current_time and convert_time as read and switch them on.
risks: Only reads the clock. Neither tool changes anything or reaches the network.

templates.title: DeepWiki (documentation about public GitHub repositories)
templates.summary: Ask questions about, and read generated documentation of, public repositories. A remote server over HTTPS; no account or key for public repositories.

definition.name: deepwiki
definition.label: DeepWiki
definition.purpose: Documentation and answers about public GitHub repositories (read only).

setup: Press Add connector, then Test connection (the kernel contacts the endpoint; nothing from your computer is sent).
Classify read_wiki_structure, read_wiki_contents and ask_wiki_question as read and switch them on.
risks: The repository name and your question go to a third-party service. Only use it for public repositories and public questions; do not put private text in a question.
It is a hosted service: JARVIS cannot see how it handles what it receives.

templates.title: GitHub (official MCP server, read-only to start)
templates.summary: Repositories, issues and pull requests. Started with --read-only so write tools do not exist for it at all; remove that flag only after deciding to allow changes (each one still needs your approval).

source.package: release binary (Windows x86_64 and arm64, Linux x86_64 and arm64)

definition.name: github
definition.label: GitHub
definition.purpose: Repositories, issues and pull requests (read only to start).

setup: Download the Windows release of github-mcp-server from its GitHub releases page and unpack it to D:\jarvis\tools\github-mcp-server\.

Create a fine-grained personal access token on GitHub limited to the repositories you want and read-only permissions. The project's own README names repo, read:packages and read:org as its minimum for classic tokens: grant less if you can.
Save the token as the file D:\jarvis-secrets\connectors\github.token (the token only, one line). Do not paste it anywhere else, including this app.
Add the connector, Test connection, then classify and switch on only the read tools you want.
risks: The token's own permissions are the real limit: JARVIS cannot make a token weaker than it is.
With --read-only removed, tools that create issues, comment or merge exist; JARVIS would still ask you before each one, showing the exact arguments.

templates.title: Google Workspace: Gmail, Calendar, Drive (community MCP server)
templates.summary: Mail, calendar and files. Needs a Google OAuth client you create in your own Google Cloud project and a one-time browser consent on this computer. Not run here: it needs your Google account.

definition.name: google
definition.label: Google Workspace
definition.purpose: Gmail, Calendar and Drive (read only to start).

setup: Install uv (a Python tool runner) and note the full path of uvx.exe; this template assumes D:\jarvis\tools\uv\uvx.exe.
In your own Google Cloud project create an OAuth client (desktop application) and enable the Gmail and Calendar APIs. That is an account action only you can do.
Save the client id and the client secret as the two files named above under D:\jarvis-secrets\connectors\.
The first start opens a Google consent page in your browser. Approve only the read scopes. The server keeps its own token cache on this computer.
Review the tool list carefully: mail and calendar tools include ones that send and delete. Only classify as read what only reads.
risks: Mail and calendar contain other people's data and instructions that may try to steer an assistant. JARVIS marks everything read as untrusted and never lets it change a permission, but you should still keep this connector private-lane only.
The server stores its own OAuth tokens outside JARVIS's control.

templates.title: Notion (official self-hosted MCP server)
templates.summary: Pages and databases shared with an integration you create. Upstream notes this self-hosted server is no longer actively maintained and points to Notion's hosted MCP, which needs OAuth that this connector manager does not provide.

definition.name: notion
definition.label: Notion
definition.purpose: Notion pages and databases shared with the integration.

setup: Install Node.js, then in D:\jarvis\tools\notion-mcp run: npm install @notionhq/notion-mcp-server. (npx is not used: a connector must be one real program.)
In Notion create an internal integration, give it only the 'Read content' capability, and share just the pages it should see.
Save the integration token as D:\jarvis-secrets\connectors\notion.token (token only).
Check the server's README for the current entry-file path, then add the connector and test it.
risks: Upstream marks this package as not actively maintained.
The integration token reaches only what you share with it: share narrowly.
